title: The sequence of primes is in many respects random

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The sequence of primes is in many respects random

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Even though the primes are generated by a simple sieving rule, the sequence of primes appears in many respects remarkably random.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the actual sequence of primes that is obtained seems in many respects remarkably random.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “The Sequence of Primes” (from p. 132), p. 133. Scope: the sequence of prime numbers

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.86

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Extensive prime data and mathematical results are publicly available, with ample scale for standard tests. Because no single random model captures the informal wording, the claim can be resolved only property by property.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use large public prime tables and proven distribution results to test specified properties such as gap distributions, residue frequencies, correlations, and unpredictability against explicit random models. Agreement on many preregistered properties supports the qualified claim, while systematic deviations identify respects in which it fails.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Primes have exact deterministic structure and known deviations from naive random models.

In many respects permits selective choice of favorable statistics.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 1.0
discriminating power: 0.72
analysis feasibility: 0.94
operationalizability: 0.72
data adequacy: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Primes are tabulated to limits that make sampling error irrelevant for any practical appearance claim, and the comparison with a random model is standard. The wording still cannot be cleanly refuted: known regularities and known random-like features both sit comfortably inside 'in many respects remarkably random.' The data are more than adequate, and the decision criterion is not.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare prime gaps, residue counts, and related prime statistics with the Cramér random model and with the prime number theorem on primes tabulated far beyond the pictures in the book. Systematic agreement on a predeclared list of statistics would support randomness in those respects; the test does not pin down 'many respects.'

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'In many respects' remains true if some statistics look random and others, such as the prime number theorem or Chebyshev biases, do not.

The sieve that generates the primes builds in modular structure, so a test can rediscover that structure or average it away depending on the statistic.
